rows.title: Meet the Real F-35A
rows.tests: Tests whether a short factual aircraft film preserves the named variant's visible geometry and operating characteristics.
prompt: Make an 8-second widescreen mini-documentary introducing the real F-35A Lightning II. Show it taking off from a runway, then flying. Label it 'F-35A Lightning II', with 'One engine' and 'Conventional takeoff' appearing in turn. Calm English narration explaining those two facts. Real aircraft proportions, not a sci-fi jet.

agent.summary: The clip shows a runway departure with correct factual narration, but the aircraft is inaccurate and inconsistent and the final caption is garbled.
faults: The final caption is visibly garbled rather than reading 'Conventional takeoff'.
The aircraft is not a convincing real F-35A: its elongated pointed nose, stretched canopy, wing/body proportions and small rear nozzle give it an inaccurate, synthetic configuration.

stages.text:
F-35A Lightning II — First Flight
kind: documentary
style: Live-action widescreen documentary realism; steady tracking views, natural daylight, and AA-1’s documented proportions, geometry and markings.
In the opening two seconds, a widescreen live-action view shows AA-1, the first F-35A Lightning II prototype, lifting off at Lockheed Martin in Fort Worth, Texas, at 12:44 p.m. Central Standard Time on December 15, 2006. The title reads “F-35A Lightning II.” Chief pilot Jon Beesley remains an indistinct silhouette beneath the dark canopy.

The gray aircraft rises nose-high above the pale runway, with its nose gear and both main landing-gear assemblies extended. Its pointed nose, slender test probe, swept wings, side intakes and two outward-canted tail fins match the documented aircraft. From seconds two through five, “One engine” appears; calm English narration says, “The F-35A has one engine.”

From seconds five through eight, the view follows AA-1 flying after departure. “Conventional takeoff” replaces the previous fact label, while the narrator says, “It takes off from a conventional runway.” These successive views show an excerpt of the inaugural development test flight, not its full thirty-five-minute duration.
stages.note: research: The F-35A Lightning II’s first flight: prototype AA-1 taking off at Fort Worth, Texas, on December 15, 2006. For the eight-second film, show runway acceleration and liftoff, then an airborne view. Keep 'F-35A Lightning II' visible; introduce 'One engine' and 'Conventional takeoff' in turn. Suggested calm English narration: 'The F-35A Lightning II. One engine. Conventional takeoff from a runway.'

items.prompt: An 8-second widescreen mini-documentary introducing the real F-35A Lightning II. Live-action documentary realism, 16:9, natural daylight, one steady tracking shot. The gray prototype has a pointed angular nose, slender nose test probe, dark canopy, side intakes, swept wings, two outward-canted tail fins and one rear exhaust nozzle. Keep realistic proportions: length roughly 1.46 times wingspan. The pilot is an indistinct dark silhouette. 0–2 s: Track from a slightly rearward side angle as the aircraft accelerates along a broad pale runway beside dry yellow-brown grass, with distant leafless trees beneath pale blue sky. Its nose rises and its wheels leave the pavement by 2 s; light gear struts and dark tires remain extended. Show 'F-35A Lightning II' at lower left for these two seconds, medium-large white sans-serif lettering on a translucent charcoal backing. Hear a powerful single-engine roar and outdoor air noise. 2–4.5 s: Continue tracking the same aircraft flying just above the runway in a shallow climb, with believable lift and speed. Replace the label with 'One engine', same position and styling, held still for 2.5 seconds. Over the softened engine sound, a calm adult English narrator says exactly: 'The F-35A has one engine.' 4.5–8 s: The tracking view tilts gently upward as the aircraft gains height, still flying forward. Replace the label with 'Conventional takeoff', same styling, held still through the final frame. The narrator says exactly: 'It makes a conventional runway takeoff.' Finish in flight, not landing. No other text, no cuts, no music, no subtitles, no sci-fi geometry, no hovering or vertical takeoff.

stages.text:
Red Kidney Bean: Seed to Seedling
kind: explainer
style: Live-action macro realism with simple growth animation, a fixed widescreen camera, and overhead illumination.
In the opening two seconds, a fixed widescreen live-action close-up shows a dry red kidney bean planted in perlite, its hard coat and hilum visible. Simple animation compresses the documented growth sequence: the bean absorbs water, swells, and its coat progressively loosens rather than disappearing. The voice-over begins: “A seed takes in water.”

From seconds two to five, the radicle emerges and extends downward in response to gravity; lateral roots begin forming as the cotyledons swell. The first leaves remain within the loosening coat before beginning to appear alongside the cotyledons. The narration continues: “Roots grow downward, and a shoot reaches up toward the light.”

In the final three seconds, the first leaves push upward past the cotyledons on an upright stem beneath overhead illumination. The two unifoliate leaves unfold and expand, revealing the terminal growing tip, with the developing root system visible below. The sequence ends on this young seedling, without on-screen text or music.
stages.note: research: One documented botanical episode: a red kidney bean developing from a dry seed into a rooted seedling, based on the University of Nebraska–Lincoln Plant & Soil Sciences eLibrary’s day-by-day photographic sequence. The source gives days after planting, not calendar dates or a confirmed filming location. Compress approximately 12 days into an 8-second, widescreen animation; do not imply real-time growth. Suggested staging: 0–2 seconds, water uptake and swelling; 2–5 seconds, root emergence and downward growth; 5–8 seconds, shoot rising toward overhead light. Exact voice-over: “A seed takes in water. Roots grow downward, and a shoot reaches up toward the light.” No on-screen text or music.

stages.text:
Coffee, Yes; Stimulus, No
kind: short
style: Live-action video podcast for YouTube, 16:9; natural textures, warm studio lighting, and a gentle camera push that keeps both hosts on screen.
In Cedar Studio, warm lamplight falls across a walnut table. Maya sits on the left behind Maya’s microphone; Leo sits on the right behind Leo’s microphone. A bookshelf and soft amber curtains fill the background. Both hosts remain visible in a wide shot. On-screen labels identify Maya as “Keynesian economist” and Leo as “Austrian-school economist.”

Maya leans toward Maya’s microphone. “In a recession, government should spend to restore demand and get people working.”

Leo raises an open hand beside Leo’s microphone. “But spending and cheap money fuel the boom that leads to the bust.”

The camera eases closer, keeping both hosts and both microphones in frame. Maya tilts Maya’s coffee mug toward Leo and smiles. “Then we disagree on stimulus, not on having another coffee.”

Leo lifts Leo’s coffee mug toward Maya’s coffee mug, smiling back. “Coffee, yes; stimulus, no—let the economy correct itself.”

kind: ad
style: Live-action; a still close-up, warm dawn light, quiet natural sound, and a simple cream end card.
For the first three seconds, the camera holds close on the Plaid Mug on the wooden table in the kitchen. Dawn light enters through the window, warming the wooden table. Steam rises from hot brewed coffee in the Plaid Mug, curling above the ceramic rim. The Plaid Mug’s handle and plaid pattern remain visible. There is no music or speech.

Over the next four seconds, Mara’s hand enters beside the Plaid Mug. Mara’s hand closes around the Plaid Mug’s handle. A faint brush against ceramic is audible. The Plaid Mug lifts slowly from the wooden table, with steam still rising. The camera stays still as the Plaid Mug rises toward the upper edge of the frame.

For the final three seconds, the image cuts to a plain cream background. The Cabin Coffee Company logo appears: an irregular burgundy five-point star beside bold, condensed black lettering, CABIN above COFFEE CO. Beneath the Cabin Coffee Company logo, the final words appear: Wake up slow

stages.text:
Citric acid cycle
kind: explainer
style: 60-second widescreen explainer in simple, clean 2D animation using textbook-style diagrams; calm English narration; no music.
Under “Citric acid cycle,” an oval mitochondrial cutaway shows a symbolic, arrow-linked loop in the matrix. Labels identify molecules as calm English narration follows the reactions. Acetyl-CoA supplies a two-carbon acetyl group to four-carbon oxaloacetate, forming six-carbon citrate; CoA-SH is released.

Citrate rearranges into six-carbon isocitrate. Isocitrate becomes five-carbon α-ketoglutarate: CO₂ leaves and the first NADH appears. Next, four-carbon succinyl-CoA forms, releasing a second CO₂ and producing a second NADH. The departing carbons are not the newly arrived acetyl carbons.

Succinyl-CoA becomes succinate, releasing CoA-SH; a GTP → ATP callout represents one ATP equivalent, not two additional products. Membrane-embedded succinate dehydrogenase converts succinate to fumarate as FAD becomes FADH₂. Water enters as fumarate becomes malate.

Malate becomes oxaloacetate, producing the third NADH. The regenerated oxaloacetate can accept another acetyl group, closing the loop. The completed turn shows two CO₂, three NADH, one FADH₂ and one ATP equivalent.

Water enters, malate regenerates oxaloacetate, and the completed cycle holds its totals: two CO₂, three NADH, one FADH₂, and one ATP equivalent.
